lead: A discrete-time LTI system is a rule that turns one sequence into another. Linearity plus time invariance lets one short sequence describe it completely: the impulse response h[n]. The output is then the convolution sum of input x[n] and h[n]. This is the discrete twin of the convolution integral. Phones, audio filters, ECG smoothing and fraud filters all run such sample-by-sample rules.
prereq: You need Chapter 5.1 for how x[n] arises, Unit 1 for δ[n], u[n] and system properties, and Unit 2 for the convolution integral that this chapter mirrors.

blocks.text: A discrete-time signal is a sequence x[n]. Here n is an integer sample index, not a continuous time. A periodic sequence has x[n + N] = x[n] for every n; the smallest positive N is its period.

The unit impulse is δ[n] = 1 at n = 0 and δ[n] = 0 elsewhere. The unit step is u[n] = 1 for n ≥ 0 and u[n] = 0 for n < 0. They relate by δ[n] = u[n] − u[n − 1]. A shifted impulse δ[n − m] is nonzero only at n = m.

The impulse response h[n] is the output of an LTI system when the input is δ[n], with the system at rest. Because the system is linear and time-invariant, an input x[n] = Σ<sub>k</sub> x[k] δ[n − k] produces a sum of shifted, scaled copies of h[n]. That sum is the convolution sum.

sections.h3: The convolution sum and two ways to evaluate it

blocks.text: y[n] = Σ<sub>k=−∞</sub><sup>∞</sup> x[k] h[n − k] = Σ<sub>k=−∞</sub><sup>∞</sup> h[k] x[n − k]
blocks.where: y[n] is the output sample at index n; x[k] is the input sample at index k; h[n − k] is the impulse response reversed and shifted by n; k is the dummy summation index.

blocks.text: For finite sequences, keep only overlapping nonzero terms. If x[n] has length N₁ and h[n] has length N₂, then y[n] has length N₁ + N₂ − 1.

items: Sliding method: plot x[k] and h[n − k]. For n = 0, flip h[k] to h[−k], place it at k = 0, multiply overlapping samples and add.
Increase n by 1. The flipped h[n − k] shifts right by one sample. Multiply the new overlap and add. Repeat until no overlap remains.
Table method: for each output index n, list the products x[k] h[n − k] for all k, then add the row. The row sums are y[n].

sections.h3: Properties, causality, stability and frequency response

items: Distributive: x * (h₁ + h₂) = x * h₁ + x * h₂.
Identity element: convolving with δ[n] returns the original sequence.

blocks.text: A causal discrete-time LTI system has h[n] = 0 for n < 0. Its output at n depends only on present and past input samples. A BIBO-stable system has Σ |h[n]| finite; every bounded input then gives a bounded output.

blocks.where: H(e<sup>jω</sup>) is the frequency response; ω is angular frequency in radians per sample; h[n] is the impulse response; j is the imaginary unit. If x[n] = e<sup>jωn</sup>, then y[n] = H(e<sup>jω</sup>) e<sup>jωn</sup>.

blocks.text: The step response is s[n] = Σ<sub>k=−∞</sub><sup>n</sup> h[k]. It is the running sum of the impulse response. The frequency response gives the complex gain at each ω; its magnitude is amplitude gain and its angle is phase shift.

figure.caption: Convolving x[n] = [2, 1, 3] with h[n] = [1, 2] gives y[n] = [2, 5, 5, 6]. The marked y[1] comes from 2·2 + 1·1 = 5.

spec.title: Convolution of x[n] and h[n]
spec.aria: Three rows of numbers: x[n] = 2, 1, 3 convolved with h[n] = 1, 2 gives y[n] = 2, 5, 5, 6, with y[1] = 2·2 + 1·1 = 5 marked.

examples.question: For x[n] = [2, 1, 3] at n = 0, 1, 2 and h[n] = [1, 2] at n = 0, 1, use y[n] = Σ x[k]h[n − k] to find y[0] to y[3]. Then test h[n] = (0.5)<sup>n</sup>u[n] for BIBO stability.
steps: List nonzero samples: x[0] = 2, x[1] = 1, x[2] = 3; h[0] = 1, h[1] = 2.
y[0] = x[0]h[0] = 2·1 = 2. Other k give no overlap.
Thus y[n] = [2, 5, 5, 6]. Its length is N₁ + N₂ − 1 = 3 + 2 − 1 = 4, which matches.
The sum 2 is finite, so the system is BIBO stable.
examples.answer: y[n] = [2, 5, 5, 6] with length 4 samples, and the system with h[n] = (0.5)<sup>n</sup>u[n] is BIBO stable because Σ |h[n]| = 2 is finite.
examples.check:
x = [2, 1, 3]
h = [1, 2]
y = [0] * (len(x) + len(h) - 1)
for n in range(len(y)):
    total = 0
    for k in range(len(x)):
        j = n - k
        if 0 <= j < len(h):
            total += x[k] * h[j]
    y[n] = total
for value in y:
    print(value)
print(len(y))
print(1 / (1 - 0.5))

traps: Not flipping h[n] in the sliding method. You must use h[n − k], not h[k], while sliding.
Losing the first or last output sample. For finite sequences check the length N₁ + N₂ − 1.
Mixing indices n and k: n is the output sample being found, k is the summation index.
Testing only the first few terms of h[n] for stability. The whole sum Σ |h[n]| must be finite.
Confusing the impulse response h[n] with the frequency response H(e<sup>jω</sup>). One is a sequence in n; the other is a function of ω.

quiz.q: Define the impulse response of a discrete-time LTI system.
quiz.a: It is the output h[n] when the input is δ[n], with the system initially at rest.

quiz.q: Why does h[n] completely describe an LTI system?
quiz.a: Any input can be written as a sum of shifted, scaled impulses. Linearity and time invariance then give the output as the same sum of shifted, scaled copies of h[n].

quiz.q: x[n] = [1, 2] and h[n] = [1, 1, 1], both starting at n = 0. Find y[n] by convolution.
Is the system with h[n] = (0.9)<sup>n</sup>u[n] BIBO stable? Justify.
quiz.a: Yes. Σ |h[n]| = Σ (0.9)<sup>n</sup> = 1/(1 − 0.9) = 10, which is finite.

quiz.q: Input x[n] = δ[n − 2] passes through h[n] = [1, −1, 2] starting at n = 0. Find y[n].
quiz.a: The output is h[n − 2], so y[n] = [0, 0, 1, −1, 2] for n = 0 to 4.

quiz.q: What condition on h[n] makes a discrete-time LTI system causal?
For h[n] = u[n], state whether the system is causal and BIBO stable.
quiz.a: Causal, because h[n] = 0 for n < 0. Not BIBO stable, because Σ |h[n]| = 1 + 1 + 1 + … diverges.

quiz.q: Write H(e<sup>jω</sup>) for h[n] = [1, 2] at n = 0, 1.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, convolution sum runs as FIR filtering in audio, software-defined radio, ECG cleanup and image blur. Fast convolution uses the FFT and overlap-add or overlap-save blocks for long signals. Search next for FIR filter, circular convolution and overlap-add method if you want the practical DSP route.
